assets.question: After reviewing Marcus's gaze behavior across the negotiation, which diagnosis best matches the observation log?
assets.subject_baseline: Marcus is a chatty account manager who usually holds steady eye contact during sales calls, blinks at an average conversational rate, and freely glances around the room while talking. T+00:11 - Diana asks about the missed quarterly forecast; his blink rate climbs to roughly double his baseline and his squinting increases. T+00:14 - Marcus looks down at the table for nearly four seconds before answering, then glances toward the door while the deadline extension is discussed. T+00:19 - While claiming the figures 'got lost in the system,' Marcus looks up and to his right, blinks rapidly, and touches the corner of his mouth with his index finger. T+00:26 - When Diana mentions rescheduling in front of her manager, Marcus finally holds steady eye contact and his blink rate normalizes.

Diana: 'Can you walk me through the numbers right now from memory?' Marcus: 'Uh... I would rather pull it up on my screen. It's a lot of detail.' Diana: 'Are you uncomfortable discussing this with me?' Marcus: 'No, no, it's fine. I just want to make sure I give you accurate figures.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Marcus is anxious and likely withholding: his sustained downward gaze indicates anxiety or submission, his elevated squinting and blink rate show increased stress, the rapid blinking paired with face-touching at the mouth is the pattern the text flags when a lie may be told, and looking toward the door reveals a desire to end the conversation.

The blink-rate spike at T+00:11 and again at T+00:19 occurs exactly while he is pressed on the missed forecast, matching the claim that squinting and blinking increase when people think hard or are stressed, and that increased blinking signals lying especially with face-touching at the mouth. His glance at the door during the deadline topic indicates a need to leave the interaction. His up-and-to-the-right look while narrating the excuse is the text's claimed sign of an invented story versus the up-and-left recall of a genuine memory. The cluster, not any single cue, points to withheld information delivered under stress, so Diana should verify his story against system records before trusting the excuse.

Marcus is fully relaxed and comfortable, since his pupils widened at several points and dilated pupils are always the mark of a confident negotiator.

assets.question: Reading the mouth cluster alone, which is the best-supported diagnosis of Mr. Okafor's state during the signing call?
assets.subject_baseline: Mr. Okafor is an expressive, warm client who laughs openly, smiles with his eyes crinkling, and gestures with his hands during routine status calls. In previous recorded calls, his smile reaches his entire face and he never cups his mouth while speaking about budgets or terms.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: T+00:05 - Small talk about his daughter's graduation; Mr. Okafor smiles broadly, cheeks lifting, corners of his eyes crinkled. T+00:09 - Priya reads the renewal clause that removes the quarterly price cap; his lips press together and thin for three seconds. T+00:12 - He agrees verbally, then bites his lower lip briefly and glances at the papers. T+00:15 - His mouth twists down at the corners while he asks 'Is that the final draft?' T+00:18 - He covers his mouth with one hand, coughs softly, and says he needs a day to 'sleep on it.' T+00:21 - Priya offers to keep the old cap; he resumes his full-face smile and leans forward in his seat.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Priya: 'The new clause removes the quarterly cap. Is that acceptable to you?' Mr. Okafor: 'Yes, that works for me. Fine.' Priya: 'You seem uncertain for someone who just said yes.' Mr. Okafor: 'Uncertain? I'm just tired. Long week. Can I take a day to sleep on it?' Priya: 'Of course. I can keep the old cap if you prefer.' Mr. Okafor: 'That... that would actually be a relief.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Mr. Okafor is expressing concealed disapproval or worry about the clause despite saying yes: his genuine full-face smile appears only during pleasant small talk, while the renewal clause triggers pursed lips, a down-turned mouth, lip-biting, and a cover-mouth reaction, all classified in the text as disapproval, worry, or concealment signals.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The baseline establishes that his real smile engages the whole face, which is the text's definition of a genuine smile. During the clause discussion he produced a mouth-only verbal approval: the wide genuine smile disappears, replaced by pursed lips ('distaste, disapproval, or distrust'), a down-turned mouth ('sadness, disapproval, or grimacing'), and lower-lip biting ('anxious, worried, or stressed'). His cover-the-mouth gesture right after agreeing is the text's marker for hiding a reaction, which can be an attempt to cover disapproval. Crucially, his full-face smile returns the moment Priya restores the old cap, confirming the genuine smile tracks satisfaction and the mouth-only smile tracked withheld displeasure. The defensive read: his verbal 'yes' contradicted his nonverbal state, so his later request for time was not a stall tactic but a genuine boundary, and Priya should confirm terms in writing before treating the deal as closed.
distractors: Mr. Okafor is delighted with the new clause: his occasional smile and quick 'yes' are the definition of complete agreement, and pursed lips merely show he is concentrating.
Mr. Okafor is about to fall ill: he bit his lip and covered his mouth to suppress a cough, and every lip signal he showed is a symptom of a cold, not disapproval.
Mr. Okafor is flirting with Priya, because covering the mouth and lowering the gaze are listed as romantic invitation cues in the chapter.

assets.topic: The Barrier Boss: Arms, Objects, and Personal Space
assets.visual_frame_description: A narrow breakroom table between two chairs. Across the table, Dario, a shift supervisor, sits with his arms folded so tightly that his shoulders hunch, holding a stack of printed schedules upright in front of his chest like a wall. Near him, a second figure, Carlos, leans far forward over his side of the table, invading the space of the seated employee opposite him. The screen labels the pose 'Barrier vs. Invasion.'
assets.player_mission: Defeat the Barrier Boss in two stages. First, identify the strongest protective signal in the observed scene. Then, when your personal space is invaded, choose the boundary-defense move that matches the chapter's guidance instead of escalating.
key_concepts: Think of a person's arms as the door to the body and the self: if a person folds their arms while interacting, it is often read as a defensive, barrier signal.
Crossed arms can demonstrate nervousness, weakness, or a shut mind.
Crossed arms combined with a genuine smile and a generally relaxed posture can instead indicate a comfortable, relaxed state.
When a person holds an object between themselves and the person they are interacting with, it is a boundary intended to dam out the other person.
Holding onto any item with both hands shows a person has closed themselves off from others.
Holding a cup very close so it looks like hugging the cup means the person is hugging themselves.
Upper body language can show signs of defensiveness since the arms could easily be used as a shield.
Leaning forward can show interest, but it can also invade a person's personal space and show the person as a threat, which is often an aggressive display.
Invading another person's personal space can have detrimental results; the best space to keep between you and others is about one and a half feet.
This kind of forward-leaning invasion is done unconsciously by powerful people as an aggressive display.
The 'Superman' readiness gesture, hands on the waist to make oneself look bigger, shows a person is getting ready to act assertively.
assets.theory_summary: The battle tests proxemics and barrier reading: crossed arms and held objects are classified in the chapter as shields that dam out the other person, while forward leaning that invades the roughly one-and-a-half-foot comfort buffer is classified as an aggressive dominance display. The defensive frame treats these cues as warnings to maintain distance and avoid escalating a space violation, per this contested popular taxonomy.

credibility.basis: Self-published compilation; untested popular claims; treat as technique taxonomy only

assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Holding the stack of schedules upright between himself and the employee, because the chapter states that holding an item between yourself and the person you are interacting with is a boundary intended to dam out the other person, and holding any item with both hands shows a person is closed off from others.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are now the seated employee. Carlos has stepped inside your one-and-a-half-foot buffer, leaning over the table toward you with palms flat, saying 'this is decided and the discussion is over.' Your body is tensing to lean forward and push back on the table yourself. Choose the boundary-defense move that matches the chapter's guidance on personal space and aggression.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Do not mirror the invasion: keep your seat and restore a full one-and-a-half-foot buffer by pushing your chair back slightly, keep your tone and posture calm, and state your position without leaning forward into Carlos's space. The chapter warns that invading personal space is an aggressive display used unconsciously by powerful people and recommends about one and a half feet between you and others, so mirroring the lean only escalates the threat display instead of defending the boundary.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The Barrier Boss combines two body-language ideas from the chapter: arms and held objects act as a physical dam that closes a person off from the speaker, and forward leaning that pierces the personal-space buffer is an aggressive assertion of dominance. Recognizing both keeps you from mistaking a shield for rudeness, and from answering an invasion with an invasion; the defensive goal is to hold your boundary without stepping into someone else's space.

assets.dialogue: Tom: 'Hold on, before you go on, you should just push the launch back a week. Easy fix.' Narration: He taps the table, glances at his phone, and leans forward. Tom: 'And honestly, you should stop doing the demos yourself, delegate those, and rewrite the cutover plan.' Narration: He pauses only long enough to pick up his fork, then adds another suggestion. Tom: 'Trust me, I have seen this a hundred times. Just do the three things I said and it will be fine.' Narration: You have finished only the first sentence of your story. Tom nods quickly, signaling his readiness to move on. Your turn to respond.
choices: 'Tom, I hear you, and I will think about the cutover plan. Right now I mostly need to get the story out for two minutes. Can you just listen?'
'No, Tom, you are completely wrong about the timeline, and everyone knows your projects slip anyway.'
'You're right. I will push the launch back and delegate the demos today. Thanks, done.'
Stay silent, smile, nod along, and mentally do the dishes while he keeps listing solutions.
assets.theoretical_principle: Undivided attention and the advice-trap: listening before solving, and the trust cost of hijacking a conversation.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 wins because it uses the chapter's exact mechanics: it acknowledges his input so he does not feel dismissed, then names the need plainly so the conversation can switch from his solutions to your story. This protects trust by refusing to let the hijack stand, and it models the listening standard, attention to the speaker rather than to what you will say next. Choice 1 punishes his advice with disagreement, trading a repair for a conflict and showing the same hijacking instinct you are complaining about. Choice 2 abandons your own judgment to end the discomfort, which rewards the takeover and leaves the real issue unheard. Choice 3 superficially complies, but silently drifting off recreates the 'not listening' failure the chapter says is what makes or breaks relationships, and it tells Tom that hijacking works.
